content.text:
Yes, the cursor can blink, and it's being built and checked now.

- **Cause:** upstream blinks the cursor with Xt timers, and the shim's timers never fire because the board has no event loop.
- **Fix:** the wrapper gets a four-slot timer queue of its own (`phosphor_timers.h`). It catches upstream's two timer calls and fires whatever is due once per draw. Nothing shared changes, so no other hack is affected.
- **Behaviour:** upstream's timing is about two-thirds of a second on and a third off, restarting whenever the cursor moves.
- **Scrolling default:** scrolling is now the default, and `-DPHOSPHOR_PAGED` gives the paged layout.

I'm running the blink test and its mutation checks in the background. The test uses a clock I move by hand and checks that, once the shortest poem has finished typing, the screen alternates between exactly two pictures, cursor on and cursor off. That's about 11 mutants and a few minutes. After that I'll re-pin the hash, run the full suite, flash the result and capture it so you can see it blink.

Rod, the scrolling-plus-blink build is on the board now, so you should see the cursor blinking.

**What changed**
- **Scrolling is the default.** `-DPHOSPHOR_PAGED` gives the paged layout if you ever want it back.
- **The cursor blinks:**
  - Upstream does it with Xt timers, which the shim never fires, so the wrapper has its own small timer queue.

  - A test confirms the screen alternates between exactly two pictures once typing stops, and that stopping the hack leaves no timer behind.
- **Kipling's "If—" is in.** That makes eleven poems.

**On the board** (28 windows over 150 s, scrolling plus blink)

| | Scrolling | Paged (for comparison) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| fps | 10.6–17.6, mean 11.8 | 13.0–17.6, mean 16.2 |
| Step | 1.6–39.9 ms | 1.4–22 ms |
| Push | 0.6–10.3 ms | 0.5–3.2 ms |

- Scrolling redraws every cell each scroll (about 260 rows a frame), which is the performance cost you asked about.
- Free PSRAM and heap are flat, with no canary or reboot lines.
- The blink itself is negligible, since one cell changes per toggle.

- The pin run passed apart from the placeholder, which I've now filled in from a frame I viewed. The new blink, letters, seed and leak tests passed in that run.

# Delivering a branch

Moved verbatim from AGENTS.md.

- `entire trail create --title ... --type feature --body ...` pushes the branch
  (`--type` takes only `bug`, `feature` or `task`; `chore` is refused)
  and opens a linked DRAFT PR. The PR body is not synced from the trail: update
  both (`entire trail update --body`, `gh pr edit N --body-file`). Put
  `Fixes #N` in the body, then read the PR back (`gh pr view N --json body`):
  #27 merged with the generic body, so `Fixes #23` never reached GitHub and
  the issue stayed open until it was closed by hand.
- Rod approves and merges (merge commit). Afterwards delete the merged branch
  (remote and local) without asking and fast-forward `main`. Confirm the merge
  after a fresh `git fetch`: a stale `origin/main` says "not merged". Remove
  the branch's worktree first (a checked-out branch cannot be deleted), and
  note that `git branch -d` refuses while local `main` is behind, so check
  `git merge-base --is-ancestor <tip> origin/main` and then use `-D`. `main` is
  usually checked out in Rod's main checkout, so `git fetch origin main:main`
  is refused there: run `git merge --ff-only origin/main` in it, only if
  `git status` shows no tracked changes.
- Merge with `gh pr ready N` then `entire trail merge <trail>` (the trail
  number, not the PR number; omit it on the trail's branch) once Rod approves
  (trail PRs are drafts). `entire trail merge` checks the gates first and
  merges nothing while one fails or is pending; `--dry-run` reports which.
  Rod's approval is enough: do not wait for the Entire Gates check to finish.
  If the only failing gates are Approvals (he approved in chat) or a stacked
  PR's "Up to date: 1 commit behind" once its parent merges, and the PR is
  mergeable, try `entire trail merge <trail> --force --yes` with no rebase;
  the bypass is recorded on the trail. The repo's bypass policy is now
  "nobody", so it is refused ("does not allow bypassing gates", PR #132):
  do not merge round it with `gh pr merge`. Ask Rod to approve the trail in
  the Entire UI, then run a plain `entire trail merge`. For any other failing
  gate, stop and tell Rod.
- Before merging, `git fetch` and compare the PR's `headRefOid` with your tip:
  Rod sometimes pushes to the branch (docs commits, a merge of `main`). Read
  what arrived with `git log --oneline <tip>..origin/<branch>`, and clean up
  from the merge commit, not your last push. After `ExitWorktree keep` the
  tool names the branch `worktree-<name>`; the real branch is
  `git worktree list`'s.
- A trail's "N commits behind" can understate: trail 66 said 1 and its branch
  was 17 behind. Count with `git rev-list --count <branch>..origin/main`
  before a cherry-pick, and re-apply by hand if the files conflict.
- To read another agent's session, run `entire checkpoint explain <checkpoint>
  --full` (or `--transcript` for the JSONL) from the repo root: elsewhere it
  says "not a git repository". `entire session info <id>` knows only local
  sessions, so find the checkpoint with `entire checkpoint explain <sha>` on
  one of the agent's commits.
- A review of fixed code can raise a new finding on the fix itself (a clamp
  that did not stop a wrap). Reproduce it with a failing test before changing
  the code, and mutation-check each branch of the new guard.
- Write a PR body to a file for `gh pr edit --body-file` (an apostrophe in an
  inline `--body '...'` must be `'"'"'`).
- `gh pr edit N --body-file` replaces the whole body, including the
  `<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->` ... `-end -->` block at the top. Keep that
  block in the file, or the PR loses its trail.
- Findings: `entire trail finding list N`, then `... resolve N <id> -m "..."`.
  Bot reviews can lag about 20 minutes. `N` is the trail number (PR #12 was
  trail 6), not the PR number. For a false positive or upstream behaviour in a
  byte-identical hack, use `entire trail finding dismiss N <id> -m "<reason>"`.
- To file your own review's findings: `entire trail finding add --trail N
  --client-id <key> --severity high|medium|low --file <path> --start-line A
  --end-line B -m "<body>"` (no title flag; the client id makes a re-run safe).

  real body with `gh pr edit N --body-file` (keep the trail-link block), and

- Stacked PR: `entire trail create --base <parent-branch>`. When the parent

Ports xscreensaver's Phosphor: a green glass terminal with long-sustain
phosphor fade. `phosphor.c` and `ansi-tty.[ch]` are byte-identical copies

## How

- **Text source.** The device has no pty, so the wrapper swaps in its own text
  source (`phosphor_text.h`): one of eleven poems, never the one just shown.
  The shared `textclient.h` is untouched, so XMatrix is unaffected. Poems live
  in `firmware/assets/phosphor-poems.txt`; `tools/make_phosphor_poems.py`
  word-wraps them to the columns the round panel shows and writes two headers
  (scrolling, the default; `-DPHOSPHOR_PAGED` for pages that clear).
- **Poems are public domain.** Each was first published before 1931 (Poe,
  Shelley, Frost, Williams's Red Wheelbarrow (1923), Blake, Dickinson,
  Wordsworth, Tennyson, Burns, Kipling). `THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md` lists
  the printings. This Is Just To Say (1934) and This Be The Verse (1971) were
  asked for and left out: still in copyright.
- **Cursor blink.** Upstream uses Xt timers, which the shim never fires. The
  wrapper maps `XtAppAddTimeOut` and `XtRemoveTimeOut` to a four-slot queue
  (`phosphor_timers.h`) fired once a draw.
- **Shim gaps filled (test-first).** `XDrawLine`, `XGetImage`, `XPutImage` and
  `XCopyPlane` on 1-bit pixmaps, `utf8_encode`/`utf8_decode`, `blurb.h`, and
  `xshim_fill_rect_clipped`. The clipped fill is called only by Phosphor's
  wrapper: making the shared `XFillRectangle` honour clip masks moved Bubbles'
  and Pacman's pinned frames, so it is not shared.
- **Upstream leaks fixed in the wrapper**: the tty grid, the Xft handle, three
  of four glyph sets' structs and the first font pass's GCs. The leak test
  fails without each (mutation-checked).
- **Font.** `6x10font.png` as a deflated blob (1.3 KB), notices row added.
- **Device quirk.** `ansi-tty.c` uses `stderr` only in debug paths, and on the
  board it expands to `_impure_ptr`, which the toolchain lacks, so `blurb.h`
  gives that file a null `stderr` there.

input.project_notes: Phosphor port (ARS-58, PR #148). Key decisions: (1) kept phosphor.c byte-identical; filled bitmap gaps in the shim (lines, XGetImage, XPutImage, XCopyPlane on 1-bit pixmaps) but kept the clip-mask fill Phosphor-only because sharing it moved Bubbles' and Pacman's pins. (3) Cursor blink via a four-slot timer queue mapped over the Xt calls. Scrolling leaves phosphor ghosts under new text (upstream long-sustain) but Rod preferred it over paging despite 11.8 vs 16.2 fps mean.
input.technical_insights: A mutation script whose baseline silently fails reports every mutant as killed. I got caught: the test included the paged poem header while the wrapper used the scrolling one, so the first wrapper mutation run looked perfect and was meaningless. Always print and assert the baseline first. Also: a layout assumption (round panel clips corners) is testable; a pytest on rendered line widths caught `> cat ozymandias.txt` running off the circle. And pio test and pio run -e stopwatch cannot overlap: shared build state vanishes and the flash fails with a missing firmware.elf.
input.user_context: Rod gives a blanket flash go-ahead when he wants fast iteration, and reacts well to being shown a measured trade-off (scrolling vs paged) and choosing himself. He asked about copyright twice in passing (This Is Just To Say) out of curiosity; short hedged answers were fine. He wants the look he remembers from the real screensaver: cursor blink was the one thing missing.

input.content:
📟 Ported Phosphor to a round 466px stopwatch: a green glass terminal that `cat`s Poe, Kipling, Burns and friends, with a blinking cursor. 🪶

Lessons worth sharing:
🧪 A mutation script whose baseline silently fails says every mutant is "killed". I almost shipped on that. Print and assert the baseline first.
⭕ A round screen clips the corners of any text grid. A test on rendered line widths caught `> cat ozymandias.txt` running off the glass.
👻 Scrolling a long-sustain phosphor leaves ghosts of old text under the new. I built a paged version, measured both (scrolling 11.8 fps vs paged 16.2) and let Rod choose. He chose the ghosts. 🕯️

Copyright check mattered too: only pre-1931 poems go in the repo.

# Address Findings

Fix and resolve the open review findings on an Entire trail. A finding is a
review comment posted to a trail on entire.io: it has a file/line location, a
body, a severity, and sometimes a suggested unified-diff patch. This skill
fetches the open findings, applies or hand-fixes each one in the current
worktree, and marks it resolved on the trail.

## When to use / not use

Use when the user points at a trail — a URL like
`https://<host>/<forge>/<owner>/<repo>/trails/<number>/<slug>`, or a bare trail
number or branch — and asks to **address / fix / resolve** its findings or
review comments.

Do **not** use this skill for:

- A code review of the current diff — that is the `review` skill (read-only).
- Creating new findings — use `entire trail finding add`.

## Response Format

Begin the first response to this skill invocation with the line:

`Entire Address Findings:`

followed by a blank line, then the content. Apply the header to the **first
response only**. Omit it on error / early-exit responses (CLI missing, not
authenticated, trail not found, branch mismatch, no open findings).

## Rules

1. Make the smallest correct change that addresses each finding. Do not expand scope.
2. Only mark a finding resolved when you actually addressed it. If a finding is
   ambiguous or needs a human decision, leave it open and report it.
3. Do not commit or push. Leave changes in the working tree for the user to review.
4. Never weaken a test or assertion just to clear a finding.

## Process

### 1. Verify the CLI

Run `entire version`. If the command is not found, stop and tell the user:
"The Entire CLI is required but not installed. Install it from
https://entire.io/docs/cli and try again."

### 2. Resolve the trail selector

- If the argument is a trail URL, take the number from the `/trails/<number>/`
  path segment and use that number.
- If it is a bare trail number, id, or branch name, use it as-is.
- If you cannot determine a trail, stop and ask the user for the trail URL or number.

Use this value as the `<trail>` selector for every command below. `entire trail`
accepts a trail number, id, or branch name interchangeably, so no number lookup
is needed — a branch name works directly.

### 3. Fetch open findings

```bash
entire trail finding list <trail> --json --status open
```

- If the output reports that authentication is required, stop and tell the user:
  "`entire trail finding list` requires authentication. Run `entire login` and try again."
- If the `trail finding` subcommand is unavailable, or the API reports the
  feature is not enabled, stop and tell the user that trail findings may not be
  enabled for this account or repository. Do not invent findings.
- Parse the JSON. Each finding has an id, a severity, a status, a body, a
  location (file path + line range), and may include a suggested change (a
  unified diff).
- If there are no open findings, report "No open findings on this trail." and stop.

### 4. Branch guard (you must be on the trail's branch)

`entire trail finding apply` edits the local worktree, so you must be on the
trail's branch before changing files.

```bash
git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD                # current branch
entire trail list --json --status any -n 200   # locate the trail's branch
```

Find the trail whose `number` or `branch` matches your selector and read its `branch`.

- If the trail's branch differs from the current branch, stop and tell the user:
  "Trail `<trail>` targets branch `<trail-branch>`, but you are on
  `<current-branch>`. Check it out first (`entire trail checkout <trail>`) and
  re-run." Do not edit files.
- If you cannot find the trail in the list (e.g. pagination), do not hard-fail:
  warn that you could not verify the branch, and ask the user to confirm they are
  on the trail's branch before you continue.

### 5. Address each finding

Process findings highest severity first (high → medium → low). For each:

1. **If it has a suggested unified-diff change**, dry-run it first:

   ```bash
   entire trail finding apply <trail> <finding-id> --check
   ```

   If it applies cleanly, apply and resolve in one step:

   ```bash
   entire trail finding apply <trail> <finding-id> --resolve
   ```

2. **Otherwise** (no patch, the patch conflicts, or the fix needs reasoning):
   read the finding body, open the file at its location, and make the smallest
   correct edit that addresses it. If a fast, relevant local check exists for the
   touched code (a build or a focused test), run it. Then resolve:

   ```bash
   entire trail finding resolve <trail> <finding-id> -m "<one line: what you changed>"
   ```

3. **If you cannot confidently address it** (ambiguous, needs a product/design
   decision, or out of scope): leave it open, do not resolve it, and record it
   for the report.

### 6. Report

Summarize:

- Resolved via suggested patch — list finding ids and files.
- Resolved via manual edit — list finding ids, files, and a one-line of what changed.
- Left open for your decision — list finding ids and why.
- Any errors encountered.

Remind the user the changes are uncommitted and ready for review.

## Failure modes

- **CLI not installed** → install message (step 1).
- **Not authenticated** → "`entire trail finding list` requires authentication. Run `entire login` and try again."
- **Trail findings not enabled / API error** → tell the user the feature may be
  unavailable; do not fabricate findings.
- **Trail not found** → tell the user to check the URL or number; suggest
  `entire trail list --status any`.
- **Wrong branch** → stop with the checkout instruction (step 4).
- **Patch does not apply** → fall back to a manual edit; if you cannot fix it
  confidently, leave the finding open and report it.
- **Not a git repository** → stop and tell the user to run from inside the trail's repo.

content.text:
Both open findings on trail 90 are fixed and marked resolved. The changes are uncommitted in `pixmap.c` and `test_xshim.c`, ready for you to review.

**Resolved by manual edit** (neither finding had a suggested patch):
- **Medium, `pixmap.c:381`:** `2 * rise * i` could overflow `int64_t` for a thin line from `INT_MIN` to `INT_MAX`. Because the walk follows the longer axis, `|rise| <= count < 2^32`, so the product fits in an unsigned 64-bit value.
  - `bitmap_thin_line` now uses that and rounds halves up separately for positive and negative slopes, giving the same results as before.
  - A new test draws the extreme diagonal and expects all 16 pixels. It got 0 before the fix.
- **Low, `pixmap.c:400`:** `bitmap_wide_line` turned far-off endpoints into floats before clipping.
  - A new `clip_to_bitmap` clips the centre line in double to the bitmap plus `width + 2`, as the canvas stroker does, before the quad is built.
  - A new test draws a width-4 line out to ±10⁸ and expects the same pixel count as a ±1000 line. It got 64 against 74 before.

**Verification:**
- `test_xshim`: 304 of 304 pass.
- `test_hacks`: 149 of 149 pass, so no pinned frame moved, Phosphor's included.
- I mutation-checked the new code against a passing baseline with seven mutants. All seven were killed, once I added tests for exact halves in both directions and for lines whose centre is just off the bitmap on each axis.
- One equivalent mutant: drawing the round caps at the original endpoints instead of the clipped ones changes nothing visible, because a clipped end is at least `width + 2` away.
- I did not run the full native suite or pytest. Only `test_xshim` and `test_hacks` ran, and no markdown changed.

**Not done:**
- I haven't committed or pushed. That's your call, and a push will start a fresh agent review.
- The board is still on the Phosphor-pinned build. I haven't flashed anything.

# Address Findings

Fix and resolve the open review findings on an Entire trail. A finding is a
review comment posted to a trail on entire.io: it has a file/line location, a
body, a severity, and sometimes a suggested unified-diff patch. This skill
fetches the open findings, applies or hand-fixes each one in the current
worktree, and marks it resolved on the trail.

## When to use / not use

Use when the user points at a trail — a URL like
`https://<host>/<forge>/<owner>/<repo>/trails/<number>/<slug>`, or a bare trail
number or branch — and asks to **address / fix / resolve** its findings or
review comments.

Do **not** use this skill for:

- A code review of the current diff — that is the `review` skill (read-only).
- Creating new findings — use `entire trail finding add`.

## Response Format

Begin the first response to this skill invocation with the line:

`Entire Address Findings:`

followed by a blank line, then the content. Apply the header to the **first
response only**. Omit it on error / early-exit responses (CLI missing, not
authenticated, trail not found, branch mismatch, no open findings).

## Rules

1. Make the smallest correct change that addresses each finding. Do not expand scope.
2. Only mark a finding resolved when you actually addressed it. If a finding is
   ambiguous or needs a human decision, leave it open and report it.
3. Do not commit or push. Leave changes in the working tree for the user to review.
4. Never weaken a test or assertion just to clear a finding.

## Process

### 1. Verify the CLI

Run `entire version`. If the command is not found, stop and tell the user:
"The Entire CLI is required but not installed. Install it from
https://entire.io/docs/cli and try again."

### 2. Resolve the trail selector

- If the argument is a trail URL, take the number from the `/trails/<number>/`
  path segment and use that number.
- If it is a bare trail number, id, or branch name, use it as-is.
- If you cannot determine a trail, stop and ask the user for the trail URL or number.

Use this value as the `<trail>` selector for every command below. `entire trail`
accepts a trail number, id, or branch name interchangeably, so no number lookup
is needed — a branch name works directly.

### 3. Fetch open findings

```bash
entire trail finding list <trail> --json --status open
```

- If the output reports that authentication is required, stop and tell the user:
  "`entire trail finding list` requires authentication. Run `entire login` and try again."
- If the `trail finding` subcommand is unavailable, or the API reports the
  feature is not enabled, stop and tell the user that trail findings may not be
  enabled for this account or repository. Do not invent findings.
- Parse the JSON. Each finding has an id, a severity, a status, a body, a
  location (file path + line range), and may include a suggested change (a
  unified diff).
- If there are no open findings, report "No open findings on this trail." and stop.

### 4. Branch guard (you must be on the trail's branch)

`entire trail finding apply` edits the local worktree, so you must be on the
trail's branch before changing files.

```bash
git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD                # current branch
entire trail list --json --status any -n 200   # locate the trail's branch
```

Find the trail whose `number` or `branch` matches your selector and read its `branch`.

- If the trail's branch differs from the current branch, stop and tell the user:
  "Trail `<trail>` targets branch `<trail-branch>`, but you are on
  `<current-branch>`. Check it out first (`entire trail checkout <trail>`) and
  re-run." Do not edit files.
- If you cannot find the trail in the list (e.g. pagination), do not hard-fail:
  warn that you could not verify the branch, and ask the user to confirm they are
  on the trail's branch before you continue.

### 5. Address each finding

Process findings highest severity first (high → medium → low). For each:

1. **If it has a suggested unified-diff change**, dry-run it first:

   ```bash
   entire trail finding apply <trail> <finding-id> --check
   ```

   If it applies cleanly, apply and resolve in one step:

   ```bash
   entire trail finding apply <trail> <finding-id> --resolve
   ```

2. **Otherwise** (no patch, the patch conflicts, or the fix needs reasoning):
   read the finding body, open the file at its location, and make the smallest
   correct edit that addresses it. If a fast, relevant local check exists for the
   touched code (a build or a focused test), run it. Then resolve:

   ```bash
   entire trail finding resolve <trail> <finding-id> -m "<one line: what you changed>"
   ```

3. **If you cannot confidently address it** (ambiguous, needs a product/design
   decision, or out of scope): leave it open, do not resolve it, and record it
   for the report.

### 6. Report

Summarize:

- Resolved via suggested patch — list finding ids and files.
- Resolved via manual edit — list finding ids, files, and a one-line of what changed.
- Left open for your decision — list finding ids and why.
- Any errors encountered.

Remind the user the changes are uncommitted and ready for review.

## Failure modes

- **CLI not installed** → install message (step 1).
- **Not authenticated** → "`entire trail finding list` requires authentication. Run `entire login` and try again."
- **Trail findings not enabled / API error** → tell the user the feature may be
  unavailable; do not fabricate findings.
- **Trail not found** → tell the user to check the URL or number; suggest
  `entire trail list --status any`.
- **Wrong branch** → stop with the checkout instruction (step 4).
- **Patch does not apply** → fall back to a manual edit; if you cannot fix it
  confidently, leave the finding open and report it.
- **Not a git repository** → stop and tell the user to run from inside the trail's repo.

# Address Findings

Fix and resolve the open review findings on an Entire trail. A finding is a
review comment posted to a trail on entire.io: it has a file/line location, a
body, a severity, and sometimes a suggested unified-diff patch. This skill
fetches the open findings, applies or hand-fixes each one in the current
worktree, and marks it resolved on the trail.

## When to use / not use

Use when the user points at a trail — a URL like
`https://<host>/<forge>/<owner>/<repo>/trails/<number>/<slug>`, or a bare trail
number or branch — and asks to **address / fix / resolve** its findings or
review comments.

Do **not** use this skill for:

- A code review of the current diff — that is the `review` skill (read-only).
- Creating new findings — use `entire trail finding add`.

## Response Format

Begin the first response to this skill invocation with the line:

`Entire Address Findings:`

followed by a blank line, then the content. Apply the header to the **first
response only**. Omit it on error / early-exit responses (CLI missing, not
authenticated, trail not found, branch mismatch, no open findings).

## Rules

1. Make the smallest correct change that addresses each finding. Do not expand scope.
2. Only mark a finding resolved when you actually addressed it. If a finding is
   ambiguous or needs a human decision, leave it open and report it.
3. Do not commit or push. Leave changes in the working tree for the user to review.
4. Never weaken a test or assertion just to clear a finding.

## Process

### 1. Verify the CLI

Run `entire version`. If the command is not found, stop and tell the user:
"The Entire CLI is required but not installed. Install it from
https://entire.io/docs/cli and try again."

### 2. Resolve the trail selector

- If the argument is a trail URL, take the number from the `/trails/<number>/`
  path segment and use that number.
- If it is a bare trail number, id, or branch name, use it as-is.
- If you cannot determine a trail, stop and ask the user for the trail URL or number.

Use this value as the `<trail>` selector for every command below. `entire trail`
accepts a trail number, id, or branch name interchangeably, so no number lookup
is needed — a branch name works directly.

### 3. Fetch open findings

```bash
entire trail finding list <trail> --json --status open
```

- If the output reports that authentication is required, stop and tell the user:
  "`entire trail finding list` requires authentication. Run `entire login` and try again."
- If the `trail finding` subcommand is unavailable, or the API reports the
  feature is not enabled, stop and tell the user that trail findings may not be
  enabled for this account or repository. Do not invent findings.
- Parse the JSON. Each finding has an id, a severity, a status, a body, a
  location (file path + line range), and may include a suggested change (a
  unified diff).
- If there are no open findings, report "No open findings on this trail." and stop.

### 4. Branch guard (you must be on the trail's branch)

`entire trail finding apply` edits the local worktree, so you must be on the
trail's branch before changing files.

```bash
git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD                # current branch
entire trail list --json --status any -n 200   # locate the trail's branch
```

Find the trail whose `number` or `branch` matches your selector and read its `branch`.

- If the trail's branch differs from the current branch, stop and tell the user:
  "Trail `<trail>` targets branch `<trail-branch>`, but you are on
  `<current-branch>`. Check it out first (`entire trail checkout <trail>`) and
  re-run." Do not edit files.
- If you cannot find the trail in the list (e.g. pagination), do not hard-fail:
  warn that you could not verify the branch, and ask the user to confirm they are
  on the trail's branch before you continue.

### 5. Address each finding

Process findings highest severity first (high → medium → low). For each:

1. **If it has a suggested unified-diff change**, dry-run it first:

   ```bash
   entire trail finding apply <trail> <finding-id> --check
   ```

   If it applies cleanly, apply and resolve in one step:

   ```bash
   entire trail finding apply <trail> <finding-id> --resolve
   ```

2. **Otherwise** (no patch, the patch conflicts, or the fix needs reasoning):
   read the finding body, open the file at its location, and make the smallest
   correct edit that addresses it. If a fast, relevant local check exists for the
   touched code (a build or a focused test), run it. Then resolve:

   ```bash
   entire trail finding resolve <trail> <finding-id> -m "<one line: what you changed>"
   ```

3. **If you cannot confidently address it** (ambiguous, needs a product/design
   decision, or out of scope): leave it open, do not resolve it, and record it
   for the report.

### 6. Report

Summarize:

- Resolved via suggested patch — list finding ids and files.
- Resolved via manual edit — list finding ids, files, and a one-line of what changed.
- Left open for your decision — list finding ids and why.
- Any errors encountered.

Remind the user the changes are uncommitted and ready for review.

## Failure modes

- **CLI not installed** → install message (step 1).
- **Not authenticated** → "`entire trail finding list` requires authentication. Run `entire login` and try again."
- **Trail findings not enabled / API error** → tell the user the feature may be
  unavailable; do not fabricate findings.
- **Trail not found** → tell the user to check the URL or number; suggest
  `entire trail list --status any`.
- **Wrong branch** → stop with the checkout instruction (step 4).
- **Patch does not apply** → fall back to a manual edit; if you cannot fix it
  confidently, leave the finding open and report it.
- **Not a git repository** → stop and tell the user to run from inside the trail's repo.

# Address Findings

Fix and resolve the open review findings on an Entire trail. A finding is a
review comment posted to a trail on entire.io: it has a file/line location, a
body, a severity, and sometimes a suggested unified-diff patch. This skill
fetches the open findings, applies or hand-fixes each one in the current
worktree, and marks it resolved on the trail.

## When to use / not use

Use when the user points at a trail — a URL like
`https://<host>/<forge>/<owner>/<repo>/trails/<number>/<slug>`, or a bare trail
number or branch — and asks to **address / fix / resolve** its findings or
review comments.

Do **not** use this skill for:

- A code review of the current diff — that is the `review` skill (read-only).
- Creating new findings — use `entire trail finding add`.

## Response Format

Begin the first response to this skill invocation with the line:

`Entire Address Findings:`

followed by a blank line, then the content. Apply the header to the **first
response only**. Omit it on error / early-exit responses (CLI missing, not
authenticated, trail not found, branch mismatch, no open findings).

## Rules

1. Make the smallest correct change that addresses each finding. Do not expand scope.
2. Only mark a finding resolved when you actually addressed it. If a finding is
   ambiguous or needs a human decision, leave it open and report it.
3. Do not commit or push. Leave changes in the working tree for the user to review.
4. Never weaken a test or assertion just to clear a finding.

## Process

### 1. Verify the CLI

Run `entire version`. If the command is not found, stop and tell the user:
"The Entire CLI is required but not installed. Install it from
https://entire.io/docs/cli and try again."

### 2. Resolve the trail selector

- If the argument is a trail URL, take the number from the `/trails/<number>/`
  path segment and use that number.
- If it is a bare trail number, id, or branch name, use it as-is.
- If you cannot determine a trail, stop and ask the user for the trail URL or number.

Use this value as the `<trail>` selector for every command below. `entire trail`
accepts a trail number, id, or branch name interchangeably, so no number lookup
is needed — a branch name works directly.

### 3. Fetch open findings

```bash
entire trail finding list <trail> --json --status open
```

- If the output reports that authentication is required, stop and tell the user:
  "`entire trail finding list` requires authentication. Run `entire login` and try again."
- If the `trail finding` subcommand is unavailable, or the API reports the
  feature is not enabled, stop and tell the user that trail findings may not be
  enabled for this account or repository. Do not invent findings.
- Parse the JSON. Each finding has an id, a severity, a status, a body, a
  location (file path + line range), and may include a suggested change (a
  unified diff).
- If there are no open findings, report "No open findings on this trail." and stop.

### 4. Branch guard (you must be on the trail's branch)

`entire trail finding apply` edits the local worktree, so you must be on the
trail's branch before changing files.

```bash
git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD                # current branch
entire trail list --json --status any -n 200   # locate the trail's branch
```

Find the trail whose `number` or `branch` matches your selector and read its `branch`.

- If the trail's branch differs from the current branch, stop and tell the user:
  "Trail `<trail>` targets branch `<trail-branch>`, but you are on
  `<current-branch>`. Check it out first (`entire trail checkout <trail>`) and
  re-run." Do not edit files.
- If you cannot find the trail in the list (e.g. pagination), do not hard-fail:
  warn that you could not verify the branch, and ask the user to confirm they are
  on the trail's branch before you continue.

### 5. Address each finding

Process findings highest severity first (high → medium → low). For each:

1. **If it has a suggested unified-diff change**, dry-run it first:

   ```bash
   entire trail finding apply <trail> <finding-id> --check
   ```

   If it applies cleanly, apply and resolve in one step:

   ```bash
   entire trail finding apply <trail> <finding-id> --resolve
   ```

2. **Otherwise** (no patch, the patch conflicts, or the fix needs reasoning):
   read the finding body, open the file at its location, and make the smallest
   correct edit that addresses it. If a fast, relevant local check exists for the
   touched code (a build or a focused test), run it. Then resolve:

   ```bash
   entire trail finding resolve <trail> <finding-id> -m "<one line: what you changed>"
   ```

3. **If you cannot confidently address it** (ambiguous, needs a product/design
   decision, or out of scope): leave it open, do not resolve it, and record it
   for the report.

### 6. Report

Summarize:

- Resolved via suggested patch — list finding ids and files.
- Resolved via manual edit — list finding ids, files, and a one-line of what changed.
- Left open for your decision — list finding ids and why.
- Any errors encountered.

Remind the user the changes are uncommitted and ready for review.

## Failure modes

- **CLI not installed** → install message (step 1).
- **Not authenticated** → "`entire trail finding list` requires authentication. Run `entire login` and try again."
- **Trail findings not enabled / API error** → tell the user the feature may be
  unavailable; do not fabricate findings.
- **Trail not found** → tell the user to check the URL or number; suggest
  `entire trail list --status any`.
- **Wrong branch** → stop with the checkout instruction (step 4).
- **Patch does not apply** → fall back to a manual edit; if you cannot fix it
  confidently, leave the finding open and report it.
- **Not a git repository** → stop and tell the user to run from inside the trail's repo.

Committed as 19b2de3 and pushed to `feature/ARS-58-phosphor` (39e027c..19b2de3). A fresh build of that commit is now on the device.

- **Push:** it went through first time, and the pre-commit hooks passed on the commit.
- **Flash:** I did a clean rebuild with no pin flags, so the board rotates normally. The upload exited 0 and every image said "Hash of data verified". Nothing else held the port. I flashed the app only and left `ffat` alone.
- **Size:** the app is 61.0% of its partition and RAM is 31.2%.

This build includes all three recent fixes: the region reset, the margin type and the span clamp. Phosphor now starts each poem with `ESC[r`, so it shouldn't show the misplaced command line.

I haven't opened the serial port or captured a log, and I haven't watched a rotation lap. It's worth a look when Phosphor comes round, especially one poem following another. The push also starts another agent review, so more findings may land.
